messages.subject: Predict continuous response with categorical predictor variable
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am using glm to predict Weight_Gain by three predictor variables (two continuous, one categorical). For the two continuous variables, I can use the predict() to predict the response holding everything except my one independent variable of interest constant. For example: 

TRat.min <- min(All.SRs.Head$TRat, na.rm = T)
TRat.max <- max(All.SRs.Head$TRat, na.rm = T)
TRat.seq <- seq(from=TRat.min,to=TRat.max,length.out=1000)

# make a new DF that varies only along the predictor of interest
newdf.TRat <- data.frame(TRat=TRat.seq,SL.YL="Season",Area=28.85)

#make a prediction, also outputting standard errors and converting those to 95% confidence limits
pred = predict(glm_model, newdata = newdf.TRat, terms = "response", se.fit=TRUE)
pred.mean <- pred$fit
pred.ci.low <- pred$fit-pred$se.fit*1.96
pred.ci.high <- pred$fit + pred$se.fit*1.96

However, I am not sure how to do that when I want to do something similar for a categorical predictor. For example, I would like to allow SL.YL (the categorical predictor) to vary between the two levels, and then predict the continuous response of Weight_Gain while holding Area and TRat constant at some median level.

Thank you for any leads!

Kristina

​

SL.YL_seq <-levels(All.SRs.Head$SL.YL)
newdf.TRat <- data.frame(TRat=median(TRat),SL.YL= SL.YL_seq, Area=28.85)

pred = predict(glm_model, newdata = newdf.TRat, terms = "response", se.fit=TRUE)
pred.mean <- pred$fit
pred.ci.low <- pred$fit-pred$se.fit*1.96
pred.ci.high <- pred$fit + pred$se.fit*1.96
Does that make sense? If all the other predictor variables are held constant, you only need to predict the continuous response variable for the two different levels of the categorical variable.

Kristina,

You're ending up with 2 point because that's all that you have in newdata, i.e. 2 rows for your 2 factor levels because you're holding everything else constant as Rosemary is pointing out.

To put it another way, your Weight_Gain response *does not* vary in a continuous manner with respect to your categorical predictor SL.YL, rather Weight_Gain varies in a discrete manner with respect to SL.YL.

If you wanted to end up with more than 2 points, you'd have to vary (at least one of) the other predictors as well.  You could do that by varying all your predictors with a call such as:

newdata <- expand.grid(TRat=TRat.seq, SL.YL=SL.YL.seq, Area=Area.seq)  ...where each "seq" is a sequence of values from min to max or the levels of a factor, respectively.  This would give you a data.frame with all of the combinations of the supplied numeric and and factor vectors.

However, it seems like you want to visualize each predictor's effect separately, in which case 2 points is all *you should* end up with for a 2-level categorical predictor such as SL.YL.

Seconding Rosemary's request, attaching some code and data would help us help you to troubleshoot.  ...that would also help us help you with plotting these categorical predictions.  FWIW, I would use ggplot2 for plotting as it handles categorical axes without any extra complication.
